subject: Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?

messages.author: 20272e5bb86852fe
messages.subject: Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
parts:
I have seen the post by Matt Tuson asking if is it possible to fit a model with a non-symmetric adjacency matrix.

I am trying to fit a BYM model for data of geographical areas that are very unevenly structured so I set the adjacency matrix for a knn (k=5). R-INLA seems to get stuck in multiple attempts to factorize the sparse-matrix and sends the message: "I will try to fix it". The model is eventually fitted.
When I run the same model using a Queen specification for the adjacency matrix, the model runs much more faster.

Although is expected that there would be differences in the regression coefficients for each specification, there are significant differences!
You can see the code and data to reproduce the models.

From these issues, I have two questions:

1. Are the results of the model with the knn specification still valid? (from the discussion of Matt's posts I didn't get a clear answer that an INLA model with a non-symmetric adjacency matrix is still correct)
2. Are the very small coefficients found in a knn specification related to the asymmetry of the adjacency matrix?

I appreciate your help and comments,
Best,  Jack.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
parts:
Hi Jack,

and adjacency matrix doesn't define a Markov random field _by_itself_,
so whether a GMRF can be defined using an asymmetric adjacency matrix
depends on _how_ the matrix is intended to be used. Precision matrices
must be symmetric positive definite matrices, which places fundamental
theoretical restrictions on what can be done.

In the full conditional distribution specifications of the Besag model
(and where the Besag model appears in the BYM), certain symmetry
properties are required, since it's not the directed conditionals that
are specified, but the full conditionals. In the previous thread, I
believe we also discussed SAR models, which _can_ be defined via
directed graphs without other restrictions on the graph structure. See
the Besag 1974 JRSSB discussion paper and the Rue and Held 2005 book
on Gaussian Markov random fields for more details of how neighbourhood
properties work in graph based Markov models.

Finn

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
parts:
The question is what non-symmetric adj matrix means, as with the
multivariate Normal, there is no such thing as non-symmetry.

If A is the non-symmetric adj matrix, I guess it will appear as AA^T,
in the prec/cov, hence its symmetric, so there exists a symmetric adj
matrix, B, say, so that AA^T = BB^T

INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if you input a non-symmetric one,
it depends on how its coded, what it means, as it assumes its
symmetric.

H

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
parts:
To link this to my answer; the AA' construction is what would appear
in a directed hierarchical tree model.
Once the joint distribution has been obtained, this can be rewritten
as a model on the undirected graph defined by the non-sparse pattern
of AA'.

The problem with using asymmetric A directly in the full conditional
distribution expressions (e.g. saying that the conditional expectation
should be a weighted average of the "upstream" neighbours") is that
this doesn't guarantee the existence of a valid joint model. The Besag
model full conditional can only look the way they do because they are
constructed in precisely such a way that they do generate a valid
joint model. The clique potentials etc in the general MRF theory
relates directly to this, so this is a well known fundamental property
of any and all Markov random field models.

Finn

parts:
Hi Havard and Finn,
Thanks for your replies.

Following on Havard's comment "INLA assumes a symmetric graph, and if you input a non-symmetric one, it depends on how its coded, what it means, as it assumes its symmetric"; I don't see any issue with the specification of the Adjacency Matrix (AM) in my code:

> temp <- knn2nb(knearneigh(map, k=5, RANN = FALSE))
> nb2INLA("LDN.graph",temp)
> LDN.adj <- paste(getwd(),"/LDN.graph",sep="")

The model is then specified as:

> formula <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adj) + x1+x2+x3
> mod <- inla(formula,family="poisson",data=data,E=Expected, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

If an asymmetric AM doesn't allow generating a valid joint model (Finn's comment),  would it be ok without including covariates x1, x2 and x3 in the model?

On the other hand, Do the estimation of very small coefficients have to do with the asymmetry of the AM. The regression coefficients from the model are: x1=0.0000; x2=0.0001; x3=-0.0004. If I use a queen specification for the AM or even if I make the AM symmetric (with the make.nb.sym function), the coefficients change significantly ( x1=-0.011; x2=0.0003; x3=0.0041 ).

with the asymmetric AM, R-INLA sends the message "I will try to fix it". Does R-INLA select a subset of neighbors that have symmetry? Or are the small coefficients related to priors specified for the fixed component and the sampler gets stuck in a narrow range of values and is not able to  explore the posterior distribution correctly?

Thanks in advance,
Jack,

Hi,

what I ment, is for the bym model, the 'graph' is assumed to be
symmetric. seen from a matrix point of view, only the upper part of it,
or the lower part of it, has to be read. which one it is, depends on
the coding. so, if you input a non-symmetric one, then you have to read
the code to figure out what is actually happening.

> The model is then specified as:
>
> > formula <- y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=LDN.adj) + x1+x2+x3

> (Finn's comment), would it be ok without including covariates x1, x2
> and x3 in the model?
no, this has nothing to do with the covariates x1..x3.

> On the other hand, Do the estimation of very small coefficients have
> to do with the asymmetry of the AM.

you can try. if the graph is non-symmetric, do

A = inla.graph2matrix(inla.read.graph(LDN.adj))
g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))

to make it symmetric (using the 'union')

> with the asymmetric AM, R-INLA sends the message "I will try to fix
> it".
it can be a bi-effect of this, try the above trick to check.

parts:
Hi Havard,
Thanks for your reply and suggestions.
I tried building the AM as you suggested and in fact it fitted the model without any issues, yet the value and direction of the regression coefficients were different (which I wasn't expecting).
I couldn't verify the structure of the adjacency matrix from the "g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))" instruction but I run another model with an adjacency matrix forced to be symmetric (using the spdep package, before converting the AM to an LDN.adj) and as I expected, the results of this other model were identical to the ones with the "g = inla.read.graph(A + t(A))" instruction.

In brief; while the suggested "union" of the AM worked in terms of running a "smooth / faster" inla model, the model did not incorporate the KNN spatial structure I wanted. In the KNN model each area has 5 neighbors while the symmetric AM (whether from a previous symmetric AM or after adjusting it with the union) has 6.2 neighbors in average.

I explored the messages sent (using the verbose=TRUE) and it looks like R-inla does some kind of approximation to fit the model with the asymmetric AM, but I couln't (also don't know how to) verify that's the case. I looked for the message "I will try to fix it" from sending inla() in the console but I couldn't find it either. Do you know what is the procedure the program follows for the "I will try to fix it".

I am sorry to keep asking these questions but in my case is imperative to use a KNN spatial structure.

Thanks in advance,

Jack

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can R-INLA fit a model using the knn algorythm ?
parts:
Hi & thanks for your email.

Using knn to define neighbours do not give symmetry, like i could be a
neigb of j, but not the oposite. The input to some of the models
requiring a graph, assumes the graph to be symmetric. How you want to
symmetrice it, its up to you but using

A+t(A)

is the union, if i~j, then we must have j~i.

The Gaussian distribution is 'symmetric' in this sense, Cor(x_i, x_j) =
Cor(x_j, x_i) and there is no way around this.

Best
H
